title: Inspection, photos and access limitations
audience: Cleaners and supervisors recording inspections and photographs of commercial kitchen exhaust work.
learningOutcomes: Distinguish documented observation, photographic evidence and access limitations.
Identify before-and-after evidence and any section that has not been seen.
Refuse to describe incomplete access as full-system verification.

instruction.heading: Three kinds of record
instruction.body: An inspection record contains three different kinds of statement, and they must not be mixed. The first is an observation: something you saw, touched within your scope, or measured with an appropriate tool, recorded as you saw it at a time and place. The second is photographic evidence: an image that supports an observation and shows where it was taken from. The third is an access limitation: a part of the system you could not see, reach or check, and the reason. Most bad records fail because one kind is written as another. A photograph of a clean hood face is treated as proof that the duct behind it is clean. A missing access panel is written as 'nothing unusual'. A report says the system was inspected when only the accessible surfaces were seen. This lesson teaches you to keep the three kinds separate, so that the owner and the competent person can see exactly what is known and what is not.

instruction.heading: Writing an observation
instruction.body: Write observations in plain, specific language. State the location using a fixed reference, such as the hood canopy, the left filter bank or the duct take-off above the cooking line, and use the same reference names on every visit. Say what you saw, not what you think it means. 'Grease film visible on the lower edge of the left canopy panel, approximately across the panel width' is an observation. 'Hood is a fire hazard' is a conclusion that needs a competent person's assessment, and it is not for the inspection record. Include the date, the time, your name, the scope reference, and the lighting condition if it affects what you could see. If you could not see a surface clearly because the light was poor, write that down as a limit.

instruction.heading: Photographs that support, not replace
instruction.body: A photograph supports the observation it is attached to. Take it from a stated position, label it with the date, the location reference and the observation number, and keep the original file unaltered. Include a reference object or the panel edge where that helps the reader judge the scale. A photograph shows only what the lens captured, in the light available, from where it was taken. It does not prove that unseen surfaces are clean or dirty, and it does not prove the absence of a defect. Where the site uses photographs, check the site's rules on what may be photographed. Photographs can show staff, customers, screens and documents, and their storage is a site decision. Store images in the approved location only.

instruction.heading: Access limitations and sections not seen
instruction.body: An access limitation is a statement that a part of the system was not seen or checked, with the reason. Common limitations include a duct run behind a fixed ceiling, a fan housing that could not be opened, a roof component that was not reached, a canopy void that was closed, or a surface blocked by equipment that the site did not move. Record each limitation as a separate entry. Name the section, say what was not seen, state why, and say who was told. Mark the section as not inspected. Do not write 'no defects found' for a section you did not see. If the owner gives permission for a later access, record the permission and the date, and leave the section open until it is inspected. An access limitation is not a finding that the section is clean, safe or compliant. It is a statement of what the record does not cover.

instruction.heading: Before and after evidence
instruction.body: Before-and-after evidence is a pair of records taken from the same position under comparable light. The 'before' record is taken before any work starts and shows the condition as found. The 'after' record is taken when the work within scope is complete and shows the condition as left. Use the same reference names, the same angle and the same light where you can. Where a surface was not cleaned because it was out of scope, the after record should say so next to the photograph. A set of before-and-after pairs shows the change within the work you did. It does not show that the whole system is clean, and it does not show that any part is fire-safe. If a before photograph was not taken, say so and record the reason.

instruction.heading: Refusing to call partial access full verification
instruction.body: Owners and managers sometimes ask for a single sentence that says the system is clean, fully inspected or fully cleaned. Where the record covers only some sections, that sentence is not accurate, and it must not be written. Offer an accurate alternative: the sections inspected, the sections not inspected, the observations made, and the limitations that apply. If the owner insists on a wording that covers the unseen sections, refer the request to the competent person and record the referral. Do not sign a statement that describes access you did not have.

procedure: Confirm the scope and the access arrangements for the visit before starting, and record them.
Before any work, walk the accessible sections and record each observation with a location reference, date, time and your name.
Take each supporting photograph from a stated position, label it, and keep the original file unaltered. Follow the site's photography rules.
Record each access limitation as a separate entry, with the section, the reason and who was told. Mark the section as not inspected.
After the work within scope, take the after records from the same positions and label them. Note any surface that was out of scope.
Write the summary using only the observations and limitations recorded. Do not use words such as fully cleaned, fully inspected or compliant.
Give the record to the owner, and keep a copy in the approved location.

workedExamples.situation: A report from a previous contractor says the whole exhaust system was '100 percent cleaned'. It has before-and-after photographs of the hood canopy and filters only. The duct take-off and the fan housing have no photographs, and the report gives no reason.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you record, and what do you refuse to write?
workedExamples.reasoning: Record that the photographs cover the hood canopy and filters, and that the duct take-off and fan housing have no evidence in the report. Mark those sections as not verified on the report you are reviewing, and record the access limitation, if you can confirm it. Do not repeat the '100 percent' wording. Refer the claim to the owner and the competent person, and record the referral. Do not describe the whole system as cleaned or inspected.

workedExamples.situation: During your visit, the duct access panel is held shut with tape and there is no panel handle. You can see the panel edge, but you cannot open it within your scope.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How do you record the panel, and what do you tell the owner?
workedExamples.reasoning: Record the panel as an access limitation with its location reference, the reason it was not opened, and a photograph of the panel as found. Record the observed tape and missing handle as observations, without judging their cause. Tell the owner that the duct section beyond the panel is not inspected. Do not open the panel to see inside it, and do not write that the duct is clean.

workedExamples.situation: You photograph a hood canopy before work. The photograph shows a grease film on the lower edge, but the upper edge is in shadow and the light is poor.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can you record the upper edge as clean, and what do you write?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. The upper edge was in shadow, so you did not see it clearly. Record the lower-edge observation with its photograph. Record the upper edge as not clearly seen because of the light, and take a second image with better light if the site allows it. Do not record the upper edge as clean.

equipmentAndPpe: Inspection record sheet with observation, access limitation and photograph sections.
Camera or phone, used under the site's photography rules.
Torch or work light, to show what the surface looks like under directional light.
Labelled photograph log, with date, location reference and observation number.
PPE as set by the site and the task risk assessment. Inspection of accessible surfaces does not, by itself, require access equipment, and any access above ground level must be referred.

commonErrors.error: Treating a photograph of one surface as proof of the condition of a hidden section.
commonErrors.prevention: Label each photograph with what it shows. Record hidden sections as access limitations, not as clean.

commonErrors.error: Writing 'no defects found' for a section that was not seen.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the section as not inspected, with the reason, and leave it open until it is seen.

commonErrors.error: Using a single sentence to describe partial access as full verification.
commonErrors.prevention: State the sections inspected, the sections not inspected and the limitations, and refuse the single-sentence wording.

commonErrors.error: Taking an after photograph from a different position, so that the before and after cannot be compared.
commonErrors.prevention: Mark the reference positions on the record and take each after image from the same position as the before image.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: NSW Fire and Rescue's restaurant guidance says that routine cleaning and inspection of hoods, ducting and grease fans is an ongoing task. The guidance does not set an inspection frequency for any site.
Photographs can capture personal information about staff and customers. Check the site's rules before taking, storing or sharing any image.

An inspection record by a cleaner is a record of what was seen and what was not seen. It is not a fire-safety inspection, a compliance assessment or a certificate. Only a competent person, eligible under the requirements that apply, may make a compliance or fire-safety assessment.

This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval or specialist authority. Opening access panels, examining ductwork or assessing fire-suppression components are specialist work and are outside this lesson.

qualityStandard: Every observation in the worked example is written with a location reference, date, time and a description that does not draw a conclusion.
Every hidden or unseen section is recorded as an access limitation with the reason and the person told, not as clean or compliant.
Before and after photographs are labelled and taken from the same reference position, or the reason for the difference is recorded.
documentationEvidence: Inspection record with separate sections for observations, photographs and access limitations.
Labelled photograph log with date, location reference and observation number.
Access limitation entries, with the section, the reason, the person told and the date.
Before and after pairs for the work within scope, with notes on out-of-scope surfaces.
summary: Keep observation, photograph and access limitation separate in every record.
Write what was seen, not what it means. Conclusions belong to the competent person.
Record each unseen section as not inspected, with the reason. Do not treat it as clean.
Refuse to describe partial access as full verification, and refer any such request.

knowledgeChecks.question: Do photographs of the visible hood surfaces prove that the whole duct was cleaned?
options: Yes, a clear photograph shows the whole system, including every part of the duct run
No, a photograph shows only what the lens captured, so the duct needs its own record
Yes, if the photographs are taken in good light from the hood and the roof

knowledgeChecks.question: A report claims 100 percent cleaning but has no photographs of a hidden duct section. How is that section recorded?
options: As clean, because the report says so and the contractor signed it
As an access limitation, with the reason and the person told, and not as clean
As a defect, because there are no photographs of that section in the file at all

knowledgeChecks.question: The owner asks you to say the system is fully inspected, when the duct and fan were not accessible. What is the correct response?
options: Write the sentence, because the owner has asked for it and is paying for the whole job today in full
Write the sections inspected, the sections not inspected and the limitations, and refuse the single sentence
Write a sentence that says the system is inspected, but leave out the limitations so the report reads well
